one-dimensional approximation introduces large errors in the prediction capability
for such flows. Moreover, temperature stratification through solid walls enhances
the uncertainties of one-dimensional approximation.

The objective of the present study is to overcome the above limitations by developing a computational tool that is able to describe the coupled hot-gas=wall=coolant
environment that occurs in most liquid rocket engines, and to provide a quick and
reliable prediction of thermal stratification phenomena in cooling channels. This goal
is achieved by an extension of one-dimensional methods still widely relying on empirical relationships. In particular, the proposed model, inspired by the approaches introduced in references [25–27], allows one to compute the radial stratification of both the
wall and the coolant temperatures by considering a quasi-2-D flow evolution through
the cooling channels, which is coupled to the radial heat transfer in the rib. The
quasi-2-D model includes a nonuniform velocity profile in the coolant governing
equations to describe with reasonable precision the wall heat flux distribution in the
radial direction. The model, aiming to study any fluid evolving through cooling channels, considers a generic equation of state and thus the coolant fluid can be either a gas,
a supercritical fluid, or a liquid. The proposed model is validated with reference solutions of supercritical methane in a straight cooling channel with different aspect ratios,
which are obtained with a CFD solver developed in references [23,24,28–30]. The
CFD solver, which is able to accurately describe the coolant flow in rocket engines,
has been previously validated against experimental data relevant to supercritical nitrogen [24] and near-critical hydrogen [31] in heated tubes. The comparison with CFD
solutions provides thorough validation of the quasi-2-D model in terms of bulk variables evolution along the channel path, as well as local variables, distribution in the
cross-section. A further validation, which also proves the capability of the proposed
model to study the cooling of an actual liquid rocket engine thrust chamber, is carried
out by the analysis of the European Vulcain engine thrust chamber including hot-gas
expansion, wall heat conduction, and regenerative cooling in high aspect ratio cooling
channels. The available data of maximum wall temperature and coolant pressure drop
are compared with the obtained results.

2. GOVERNING EQUATIONS FOR THE COOLANT FLOW

The cooling channel flow model is developed by using the steady-state conservation laws of mass, momentum, and energy, taking into account the effects of heat
transfer and friction. In particular, the mass and momentum governing equations
are written in a one-dimensional form, whereas a simplified arrangement of the 2-D
energy equation is considered. In fact, in the case of a high aspect ratio cooling channel
with asymmetric heating, the thermal stratification that arises is strongly pronounced
in the radial direction [6,19–21], and thus the fluid energy equation can be reduced to a
2-D balance in the streamwise direction x and radial direction y (Figure 1). For that
reason, this flow model is referred to as quasi-2-D. Moreover, to accurately describe
the wall heat flux, the axial component of the fluid velocity u and the wall temperature
Tw are assumed to vary along the y direction. Similar to 1-D analysis, the transverse
velocity components v and w (radial y, and circumferential z directions, respectively)
are neglected because they are much smaller than u. According to the above

TEMPERATURE OF ROCKET ENGINE COOLING CHANNELS 5

hypotheses, the fluid pressure only depends on the streamwise coordinate position
p ¼ p(x), whereas the fluid temperature and axial velocity and wall temperature are left
to vary in a radial direction: T ¼ T(x, y), u ¼ u(x, y), and Tw ¼ Tw(x, y). As a consequence, the derived thermodynamic properties, such as density and enthalpy, and
the fluid molecular properties depend on both x and y. Finally, it is assumed that
the velocity dependence on x and y can be expressed by separation of variables as

uðx; yÞ ¼ umhðxÞ � F ðyÞ ð1Þ

where the function umh(x) represents the velocity at channel middle height, while the
function F(y) represents the shape of the velocity profile, which is also assumed to
depend on the temperature field.

The goal of the proposed quasi-2-D flow model is to describe HARCC with
more detail than the 1-D model because of the energy balance discretization in the
radial direction. On the contrary, the standard 1-D flow model takes into account
only a single fluid temperature in a channel cross-section, thus failing in the description of flow-fields with strong temperature differences.
